title: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34)
hook: for they know not what they do

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughters of Jerusalem: on the road, he turned to the women and answered their tears. Your line was weep for yourselves. Whose day did you notice, even on a heavy one? Day four hundred eighty-five.

The place is called Calvary, the skull. Two criminals are led out with him, one on his right and one on his left. Luke tells it almost without detail. They crucified him there. No description of nails, no long account of pain. The soldiers are doing a job they have done before. They will soon be throwing dice for his clothes. And into that ordinary cruelty, the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross is not a cry of pain and not a curse. It's a prayer, and it begins with today's word.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED CALVARY.` → `TWO CRIMINALS, ONE EACH SIDE.` → `THE FIRST WORD FROM THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus said: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Start with the first word. Father. Jesus has called God Father all through Luke: at twelve in the temple, I must be about my Father's business; in the garden, Father, if thou wilt. Now, nailed to wood, he still prays the same way. The relationship holds, even here. Then the request. Forgive them. Who is them? Luke doesn't say. The soldiers, surely, who are doing the nailing. Many readers widen it to everyone who brought him here. And then the reason: they know not what they do. Not that it's fine. Not that it doesn't matter. Only that they don't fully see what they're doing. Catholic devotion counts this as the first of the Seven Last Words, the seven sayings of Jesus from the cross gathered from all four Gospels, and many parishes still keep a three-hour service on Good Friday preaching on them one by one. Here's something worth knowing honestly. This verse is missing from some of the oldest Greek manuscripts of Luke. Many others have it, the Latin Vulgate has it, and the Church has always prayed and preached it as Luke's. Scholars still discuss how it came to be missing. And Luke shows it took root early: in Acts, the deacon Stephen, dying under stones, prays nearly the same prayer for the people throwing them. It's the hardest forgiveness there is, the kind given while the hurt is still happening.
screen: `FATHER, EVEN HERE.` · `FORGIVE THEM: WHO IS THEM?` · `THE FIRST OF SEVEN LAST WORDS.` · `STEPHEN PRAYS IT TOO.` · then, large: `FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone who doesn't know. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who hurt you without understanding it. A parent who said the wrong thing. A friend who never noticed what they missed. A stranger who was careless. They may never know. Hold them in mind and try the words they know not. It doesn't excuse what happened, and it doesn't mean you have to go back. If you pray, you can use the prayer from the cross for them. If not, just loosen your grip a little. The bell holds the time.
Father. The first word of the first saying from the cross in Luke: Father, forgive them. In Greek, pater. Today's word.
Your line: they know not. Today, when someone hurts you without seeing it, say it once to yourself before you answer. Day four hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 23:34 in the Passion on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke, and many parishes keep a Good Friday devotion on the Seven Last Words, of which this is counted the first.

options: a curse on the men doing it.

fork.reveal: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." the first word from the cross in Luke is a prayer for the people causing the pain.

original.note: Greek: Father, the first word of the prayer from the cross in Luke 23:34.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiveness means saying it didn't matter.
what it means: Jesus asks forgiveness for people who don't see what they're doing, while they're still doing it.
what a scholar hears: the verse is absent from some of the oldest Greek manuscripts but present in many others and the Vulgate; Acts 7:60 has Stephen echo it.
